Messages.Author: David Joseph Greenbaum
Messages.Body:
Just a quick question for the group on a couple of cards - our gaming
group is thinking of banning Peace of Khetamon and Banishment, with
regards to their ability to remove vamps from play with only a vote.
Especially banishment, with its abilirty to remove vampires from the game
and costing transfers and pool if that vampire is not at capacity when
banished. I have no problem with this cards, seeing as it is a vote card
action, that can be blocked, and a vote, which can be voted down , but my
gaming partners are of the opinion that the card's effect is unbalanced
with regards to its costs. (Vote decks should not be able to get rid of
vampires, especially with a vote card that has no minion restrictions...
which I disagree with greatly). I am on the anti-ban side of the
discussion, as I am trying to develop an effective Masquerade Enforcement
- Banishment - Anarch Revolt vote deck.

Opinions on the brokenness of Banishment, please, as our Inner Jyhad
Cabal will be voting on this...

Dave G.

Just to make the point, let's compare Banishment, to Regaining the Upper
Hand. Both of these cards are votes. Neither requires a Prince or
Justicar. Both can be blocked, voted down, etc. in the exact same way.

Regaining the Upper Hand gives you the edge.

Banishment effectively removes a vampire from the game, possibly
requiring a player to spend transfers and/or pool to be able to continue
playing the game.

There is no reason why a vote should be able to have such an effect.

> (Vote decks should not be able to get rid of
> vampires, especially with a vote card that has no minion restrictions...
> which I disagree with greatly).

You seem to disagree with this for the sole reason that you like playing
with the card. I'm sure people would get a kick out of playing Thoughts
Betrayed, too, but that doesn't make its effect balanced. In fact,
Banishment's effect is similar to that of TB, since it
removes/diminishes one's capacity to simply play the game (in one case,
to play cards, in the other, to have vampires) for a very low cost.

Messages.Author: David Joseph Greenbaum
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin (je...@cornell.edu) inscribed in fleeting electrons:
: Just to make the point, let's compare Banishment, to Regaining the Upper

: Hand. Both of these cards are votes. Neither requires a Prince or
: Justicar. Both can be blocked, voted down, etc. in the exact same way.

Agreed.

: Regaining the Upper Hand gives you the edge.

RtUH is a wall paper card - has been long since... eternity.

:
: Banishment effectively removes a vampire from the game, possibly

: requiring a player to spend transfers and/or pool to be able to continue
: playing the game.

No - it does not prevent the player from playing the game... The vamp
that's the announced target of Banishment can block. Any vamp of either
predator or prey of Banishment minion's controller can block. The vote
can be voted down. And, to boot, the vampire and the blood on the vampire
at the end of the contigently successful vote are still there...
Effectively, the only things screwed with are the transfers in the
turn(s) used to bring the vamp out. The vampire is guaranteed to come
back out before the turn of the player playing banishment, if the vampire
is full, or within four pool of full, and the effect of the vote has
been: to wit remove a vampire from play for *one* turn, and force the
player to reinfluence the vampire (if necessary) to return the vampire to
play. This is *not* "put your hand down and go get a coke." This is a
valid card, in a valid strategy, with a valid effect.

The action is not guaranteed, and it is one action (political action) to
one vampire. I see no reason why this is broken. And the vampire that
have to call votes must survive the combat monsters and the bleeders in
order to call those very votes... I see nothing wrong with Banishment.

: There is no reason why a vote should be able to have such an effect.

Straw man... RtUH is a useless card. Banishment is a useful, if non
broken card. Better to compare Banishment to, say, Conservative
Agitation, or Kine Resources Contested, which both have the effect of
destroyed pool at the cost of an action and a card. Banishment is NOT
broken when compared to these staples of the vote deck.

:
: You seem to disagree with this for the sole reason that you like playing

: with the card. I'm sure people would get a kick out of playing Thoughts
: Betrayed, too, but that doesn't make its effect balanced.

Ummm, no. I pointed out to you all of the costs, dangers, and
consequences of using Banishment as written. None of that has to do
with whether I enjoy playing that card. Banishment is not Thoughts
Betrayed. It does not break the basic values of the game. It is part of
the game.... See above.

And, even if I got a kick out of playing Banishment, does that have
anything to do with the price of tea in China? If pleasure upon the
playing of the card was the sole measure of the card's merit, then we
should ban Immortal Grapple, Decapitation, Strike: Combat Ends, and
practically any other card in the game worth playing with, in a game
meant to be played because it is fun.

: In fact, Banishment's effect is similar to that of TB, since it

: removes/diminishes one's capacity to simply play the game (in one case,
: to play cards, in the other, to have vampires) for a very low cost.

It does not. The effects of TB are inescapable except to play TB first,
and TB prevents you from using your hand - a resource in the game.
Effectively, for the cost of two blood, you are saying that your opponent
may not play the game. The consequences of playing TB, in any reasonably
designed TB deck, is a burned vamp and the loss of all the blood on it.

Your vampire Banished is not prevented from being used for purposes
either before the vote (in intercept or reaction), during the vote (inherent
votes, reaction cards) or after the vote (vampire merely uncontrolled,
not destroyed, blood still existent on vampire, etc...) If the poor vamp
isn't going to come back out during the Meth's next influence phase
because of lack of blood, well, hell's bells, it *used* that blood for
*something* (even to prevent burning in rush combat). Banishment isn't
broken because of its effect because if Banishment is broken
because you claim it is a trump, than both Immortal Grapple and S:CE are
also broken. Hell, stealth's broken then (no intercept deck can beat a
stealth bleed/vote deck)

Your argument in the light of these facts is rather specious.

Phrase it better.

>

> Just to make the point, let's compare Banishment, to Regaining the Upper
> Hand. Both of these cards are votes. Neither requires a Prince or
> Justicar. Both can be blocked, voted down, etc. in the exact same way.

You pick the weakest vote from the base set. Include Conservative
Agitation and Disputed Territory in the comparison.

>
> Regaining the Upper Hand gives you the edge.

> Banishment effectively removes a vampire from the game, possibly
> requiring a player to spend transfers and/or pool to be able to continue
> playing the game.

Banishment does not "require" the player to spend pool to continue
playing (unless he only had one vampire, in which case he was either
about to lose anyhow, or was going to spend more pool regardless).
Banishment also usually gives that player the option to spend
transfers to *gain* pool (from the Banished vampire).

The pool to be spent is also based on how much blood the vampire had
lost, something which a voting deck can usually not influence. So,
since the vote deck doesn't have precise control over the "required"
pool loss, the effect is greater in other ways for balance.

ConsAg costs a Meth 4pool in a five-player (tournament) game.
This pool loss is immediate and completely controlled by the
vote deck. It also allows the vote deck to weaken (by 1pool)
any other player at the table.

Disputed Territory does better than "removes" a location from the
game - it switches control of the location. Net change of 4pool
when used on HG, the most common location seen in my group's
games, and useful to any deck.

> There is no reason why a vote should be able to have such an effect.

Nor any reason why a vote should have Disputed Territory's effect,
I suppose?

> > (Vote decks should not be able to get rid of
> > vampires, especially with a vote card that has no minion restrictions...
> > which I disagree with greatly).
>

> You seem to disagree with this for the sole reason that you like playing
> with the card. I'm sure people would get a kick out of playing Thoughts

> Betrayed, too, but that doesn't make its effect balanced. In fact,

> Banishment's effect is similar to that of TB, since it
> removes/diminishes one's capacity to simply play the game (in one case,
> to play cards, in the other, to have vampires) for a very low cost.

And Disputed Territory: to have locations.
And ConsAg: to have pool.

But, in the case of Banishment, your ability to "have" vampires is
more under your control, since the vote deck can't usually force
you to remove blood from your ready vampires.

--

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
David Joseph Greenbaum wrote:
>
> : Banishment effectively removes a vampire from the game, possibly
> : requiring a player to spend transfers and/or pool to be able to continue
> : playing the game.
>

> No - it does not prevent the player from playing the game... The vamp

> that's the announced target of Banishment can block. Any vamp of either
> predator or prey of Banishment minion's controller can block.

Well, I guess it's just too bad if you decide to Banish the vampire
across the table. What, no Eagle's Sight? Sorry...

> The vote
> can be voted down.

_Any_ vote can be voted down. The whole purpose of a good vote deck is
to have a way to make the votes pass. The vote can in no way be voted
down when you have 4 weenie vampires, all with titles, all with
presence.

> And, to boot, the vampire and the blood on the vampire

> at the end of the contigently successful vote are still there...
> Effectively, the only things screwed with are the transfers in the
> turn(s) used to bring the vamp out.

The vampire is not in play for however long, whether it be until the end
of the game or even just one turn.

> This is *not* "put your hand down and go get a coke."

It's hard to play cards from your hand with no ready minions. It's hard
to participate in the game when your only effective 8 point vampire who
happens to have spent most/all of his blood is removed from play by a
vote called by the 1-capacity Prince of Whatever across the table.

> This is a
> valid card, in a valid strategy, with a valid effect.

Valid simply because it was printed? How is this effect justified?

> The action is not guaranteed, and it is one action (political action) to
> one vampire.

If you had 10 Banishments you would play 10 Banishments. If you wanted
the votes to be unblocked, you would use stealth. Oh, wait. You do.
So you are playing a stealth-vote deck, with presence, and you claim
that your votes, at +3 stealth can be blocked, and even if they're not,
you only have at least 5 votes in favor...

One card should not require someone to play a certain kind of deck to be
effective. Banishment effectively removes the ability of the two
strategies Bleed and Combat to deal with voting. Bleed will try to oust
it's prey before the votes kill it. Combat will try to kill the
voters. Neither of these can be done without vampires in play. Even if
Banishment just slows down these decks, especially in the case of a vote
deck, speed is everything. When you can Conservatively Agitate someone
for 16 in one turn, a delay of one turn, or the loss of transfers can be
deadly.

> I see no reason why this is broken. And the vampire that
> have to call votes must survive the combat monsters and the bleeders in
> order to call those very votes... I see nothing wrong with Banishment.

Banishment is not combat defense. Nor is it bleed defense. Just
because you feel like you don't have any other option either means that
you're uncreative, or simply paranoid.

> : There is no reason why a vote should be able to have such an effect.
>
> Straw man... RtUH is a useless card. Banishment is a useful, if non
> broken card. Better to compare Banishment to, say, Conservative
> Agitation, or Kine Resources Contested, which both have the effect of
> destroyed pool at the cost of an action and a card.

Fine. Let's compare it to KRC (since it causes a fixed pool loss,
whereas ConAg is variable). KRC: You tap a vampire, play a card, I lose
3 pool. Banishment: You tap a vampire, play a card. One of my vampires
(likely one who has blood << capacity) is moved from controlled to
uncontrolled. At worst, this causes the loss of up to 11 pool, and 3
turns' worth of transfers. But I'll consider an average case. Let's
say it only cost me 4 pool and 1 turn of transfers. Already the loss is
greater than KRC. But this doesn't take into account the loss of a
vampire. Even if I choose to spend the pool and time to bring the
vampire out, that's time that I was less able to play the game.

It's not the same, as LSJ posits, as stealing a location. You don't
need locations to play the game.

"But," you say, "you don't have to spend the pool." Sure, I could just
increase the effect of Banishment to "Choose a vampire. Remove that
vampire from the game. Any blood on that vampire is moved to it's
controllers pool, but really slowly." If Banishment _actually_ said
that, it would be even more horrible.

> Banishment is NOT
> broken when compared to these staples of the vote deck.

No, it only causes a comparable pool loss, time loss, and the (possibly)
temporary removal of a vampire from play. Strictly more powerful, I'd
say.

> : You seem to disagree with this for the sole reason that you like playing
> : with the card. I'm sure people would get a kick out of playing Thoughts
> : Betrayed, too, but that doesn't make its effect balanced.
>
> Ummm, no. I pointed out to you all of the costs, dangers, and
> consequences of using Banishment as written.

Costs which are no more restrictive than for any other vote.
Consequences? Other than people getting mad at you...

> None of that has to do
> with whether I enjoy playing that card. Banishment is not Thoughts
> Betrayed. It does not break the basic values of the game. It is part of
> the game.... See above.

It is part of the game, just because WotC printed it? There was no such
effect in Jyhad, in the original set. What other balancing measure do
we have to go by?

> And, even if I got a kick out of playing Banishment,

It might mean that you're not looking at this objectively.

> : In fact, Banishment's effect is similar to that of TB, since it

> : removes/diminishes one's capacity to simply play the game (in one case,
> : to play cards, in the other, to have vampires) for a very low cost.
>

> It does not. The effects of TB are inescapable except to play TB first,

Well, you need to have superior Dominate, and two blood. To make TB
effective, you also have to some way to exploit the fact that your
opponent can't play any cards. This requires at _least_ one other
discipline, and more cards.

Banishment require the acting minion to be a vampire. To make
Banishment effective, you also need a way to make the vote pass, so you
need, say, superior Presence. Maybe Praxis Seizures, so you can have
more votes. There's no need to exploit Banishment's effect. It effect
is exploitative enough.

> and TB prevents you from using your hand - a resource in the game.

Gosh, and vampires aren't a resource in the game?

> Effectively, for the cost of two blood, you are saying that your opponent
> may not play the game. The consequences of playing TB, in any reasonably
> designed TB deck, is a burned vamp and the loss of all the blood on it.

The consequences of Banishment, in any reasonably designed vote deck, is
the removal of a vampire from play.

> Your vampire Banished is not prevented from being used for purposes
> either before the vote (in intercept or reaction), during the vote (inherent
> votes, reaction cards) or after the vote (vampire merely uncontrolled,
> not destroyed, blood still existent on vampire, etc...)

But, oh, no! I wasn't playing an intercept deck or a vote deck. I
lose! I was playing with a titled vampire, so let's see... I've got 2
votes against. How many in favor? 10? Oh, well.

Your vampire being Thoughts Betrayed isn't prevented from using
equipment or other cards in play. And besides, unless I have a huge
card-intensive combo, _nothing_ happens to the opposing vampire.
Banishment requires one card, _maybe_ two.

> If the poor vamp
> isn't going to come back out during the Meth's next influence phase
> because of lack of blood, well, hell's bells, it *used* that blood for
> *something* (even to prevent burning in rush combat).

So I should be punished for using blood off of my vampires. You're
right. After a while using my vampires, once they don't have much blood
left, I hate having them hunt. I'd much rather have them removed from
the game.

> Banishment isn't
> broken because of its effect because if Banishment is broken
> because you claim it is a trump, than both Immortal Grapple and S:CE are
> also broken. Hell, stealth's broken then (no intercept deck can beat a
> stealth bleed/vote deck)

When is Immortal Grapple effective? When you can get to close range,
and the opposing minion was going to use a strike other than a hand
strike anyway.

When is S:CE effective? Almost always, barring use of one of the few
anti-S:CE cards. S:CE is very nearly a trump, but it's hard to justify
doing something about it when there are so may such cards.

Stealth? Come on. If you're not an intercept deck, you ignore the
stealth. Stealth alone doesn't affect someone's ability to play the
game.

> Your argument in the light of these facts is rather specious.

So, let me review your "facts". You claim that a particular vote is not
out of line, since, like every other vote, it can be blocked or voted
down. You keep saying this, over and over.

But what about a non-intercept, non-vote deck? Why should one card
cripple the ability of Bleed and Combat to deal with Vote?

> Phrase it better.

Yes, sir.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Dave Greenbaum wrote:
"Better to compare Banishment to, say, Conservative
Agitation, or Kine Resources Contested"

Yes, and when compared to KRC, for instance, Banishment comes out far
better than a card that is somewhat dubious to begin with. KRC will cause
one player (probably your prey) to lose 3 pool and another (probably your
predator) to lose 1 pool. With a cost of 1 card and 1 action that any
vampire can call, this is fairly reasonable. Now compare this to
Banishment, which has the exact same cost (1 card, 1 action, any vampire
can call it) and will on the average have the exact same effect (costing
your prey 3 pool, give or take), as well as costing the player who has a
vampire Banished transfers to get the vampire out again and causing them
to lose actions by having the Banished vampire out of play for 1 or more
turns.

Ok, Banishing a vampire may not cost your prey 3 pool, like KRC does, but
in all likelyhood it will cost at least that much to get the vampire back
into play again. This is effectively costing the player with the Banished
vampire +/-3 pool, just like KRC, for the exact same cost. Now, add onto
this effect the loss of transfers (wasted time/resources) and the loss of
actions (from the vamp being out of play for a turn or two), and
Banishment becomes way more useful (in terms of cost/effect) than KRC.

I completely agree that comparing the effect of Banishment to the effect
of Regaining the Upper Hand is completely pointless, as RtUH quite simply
blows, but comparing Banishment to KRC is perfectly valid, as both are
very useful cards, but Banishment is simply far and away better (while
accomplishing the same goal-causing pool loss to a player) and more useful
then KRC for the _exact_ same cost.

The difference is that the vote deck controls what is lost with
KRC and ConsAg. With Banishment, the vote deck is at the mercy of
the Prey to bring out larger vampires and to allow those larger
vampires to lose blood.

Since you lose control, the balance is maintained by increasing
the effect.

Malk Dementia is a more effective way of removing a Meth's
vampires, but it depends on that Meth bringing out Malks,
and on being able to use those Malks to diablerize.

Since so much of this is not under the control of the Meth, the
effect of Malk Dementia (burning a Malk, without giving his
blood back to his controller) is greater.

LSJ wrote:
"The difference is that the vote deck controls what is lost with KRC and
ConsAg. With Banishment, the vote deck is at the mercy of the Prey to
bring out larger vampires and to allow those larger vampires to lose
blood."

Yes, but then Banishment is more versitile, so it evens out on that level
(Banishing your Predators Vamp is generally much more useful than KRCing
your predators pool). Some vampire of your preys will always be down some
blood, and then by calling Banishment on them, you give your prey a
choice:

A. Have a vamp (a very important basic resource) removed from play
permanently.

B. Pay the pool to get them back into play.

If they chose "A", you have removed a vamp from the game with very little
cost (even less cost than Archon Investigation, a card widely regarded as
broken and overpowered). If they chose "B", you have effectively cost
them as much as a KRC (if not more), as well as making them waste
transfers and losing vampire actions, making the card far more effective
than KRC for its cost. Yes, under option "A" the player with the Banished
vamp may get some pool back, just like Golconda, but even Golconda gives
the player an out (pay 2 pool to avoid gaining 8).

Yes, some times Banishment will be mostly useless (and even this is highly
debateable) as neither your predator or prey will have a single vampire
with any missing blood, but most of the time Banishment will be more
effective than the basic staple vote card (KRC, a card that has already
been deemed as somewhat overpowered-Its replacement in Sabbat was Screw
the Masquerade which sucks a great deal in comparison) for the exact same
cost. Granted, it seems somewhat iffy that you could build a deck with
nothing but Banishment for offense (and again, I bet you probably could.
Imagine, if you will, the arctypical weenie vote deck with Banishments
replacing all the KRCs. No one at the table will ever take an action
again...) like you could with KRC, but a deck with, say, 10 KRC and 10
Banishment as offense will be much more potent, versitile, and IMO
sucessful than a deck with 20 KRC, which is already very potent.

Richard Braxton wrote:
"Why ban or modify any card? The game keeps it's own balance by not
letting any strategy win out over all others."

That is good in theory, but certain "broken" cards tilt the table of play
in one direction or another, and given a consistent play group (like we
have), we can endavour to "fix" various cards that we (as a group) view as
"broken" or " degenerate". After the initial relase of Jyhad, the amount
of effort put into playtesting seemed to lessen, and as a result, the
number of "broken" cards in the expansions is much greater than the number
of "broken" cards in the original set, so we decided to fix them (keep in
mind that various players in our group play, like, 5 or 6 multi player
games a week, and have for about 2 years, so we have over analiyzed and
thought about this game quite a bit). For instance, some "broken" cards
we have dealt with are:

Wake With Evenings Freshness: This card has been viewed as broken forever
(not in a game breaking way, but still a bit off) because of its complete
lack of cost and unrestricted ability to cycle. As the card reads, you
can, just to get the card out of your hand, play WWEF in response to
someone across the table calling a vote or something, not even attempting
to block. There is no cost to this. We fixed it to say that you must
attempt to block or react to play WWEF (similar to Forced Awakening, the
WWEF replacement).

Thoughts Betrayed: This card has been beaten to death (and then beaten
some more) on this newsgroup, and the general consensus is that it is just
plain wrong. Our group mutated it into a card that prevents all strikes
for a round, keeping it perfectly viable as a combat defense but
preventing the Tremere "I play TB and then procede to burn you" syndrome.

Pulled Fangs: Originally (in Jyhad and not VTES), this card just sent you
to torpor (along with the hunting problem). With the refitted Aggro rules
in VTES, Pulled Fangs became a rediculously powerful card, far outweighing
its cost (of nothing), as every combat that ended with a Pulled Fangs
resulted in a burned vampire, with no blood hunt or consequences
whatsoever (at least Decapitate only works with POT, costs 2 blood, and
the vampire needs to be going to torpor). We changed it to operate the
same way as Disarm (the PF replacement) from Sabbat, i.e. it just sent you
to torpor, like it did originally (read Disarm and compare it to Pulled
Fangs).

Archon Investigation: Another card that has been beaten quite to death in
this forum. The general consensus (among we right thinking people ;-) is
that AI is completely overpowered compared to its cost (as it saves you
pool from the bleed and burns a vampire, costing only a master card) and
the only way to avoid it is to bleed for 3 or less every action (you can't
play Sudden Reversal to stop a AI, mind you). As I assume the original
intent of this card was to slow down S+B, it failed as good S+B decks can
bleed you for 3 an action over and over again and kill you very
efficiently, while a Bruise and Bleed or Tap and Bleed deck that can only
manage to bleed you once or twice occasionally gets completely screwed.
Sadly, our group is yet to do anything about this card, as Josh and I just
recently got voted down (I think it was a tie, and tied votes fail, ya
know...)

We have recently added to cards we wanted to do something about
Banishment, Peace of Ketehmon (which is completely inferior in every way
to Banishment, yet printed after Banishment...), Protect Thine Own, and
Anathema. We banned PTO outright, and made the other 3 only work on
younger vampires than the acting one (so Igo the Prince of London can't
Banish Arika...), from whence this thread sprang.

James Hamblin <je...@cornell.edu> writes

>Fine. Let's compare Banishment to KRC (since it causes a fixed pool
loss,
>whereas ConAg is variable). KRC: You tap a vampire, play a card, I lose
>3 pool. Banishment: You tap a vampire, play a card. One of my vampires
>(likely one who has blood << capacity) is moved from controlled to
>uncontrolled. At worst, this causes the loss of up to 11 pool, and 3
>turns' worth of transfers. But I'll consider an average case. Let's
>say it only cost me 4 pool and 1 turn of transfers. Already the loss is
>greater than KRC. But this doesn't take into account the loss of a
>vampire. Even if I choose to spend the pool and time to bring the
>vampire out, that's time that I was less able to play the game.

Banishment costs no pool. All your pool is still there; the question is
how many transfers must you use to get the pool on that vampire back in
action, either by refilling the vampire or by withdrawing the pool. If
the vampire is down by 4 blood, you lose 1 action with that vampire
(roughly worth 1 pool) and 4 transfers to bring it back out. Transfers
aren't precisely costed, and their value clearly changes over the course
of the game, but I can't see that being worth more than 2 pool. So the
net cost is 3 pool - a match for KRC.

You can get a larger cost if the vampire is down more than 4 blood. If
it's down 8, you get a six pool cost - except that then you just pull off
the remainder for a cost of, say, 2 pool worth of transfers. Yes, the
vampire isn't going to be around any longer, but any vampire down 8 blood
is normally not going to be around much longer anyway.

The main kind of decks really hurt by banishment are drain-and-refill type
decks (i.e. Minion Tap/5th Tradition). I have no problem with weakening
those a bit. It does also hurt the must-have-one-vampire decks, but
that's not unbearable.

So you have a vote that costs from 1 to six pool, depending on
circumstances, and usually towards the low end. Certainly nice, but no
killer. Roughly comparable to Conservative Agitation.

Ah, well, if your position is that Banishment's argument is substantially
inferior because it only takes one of your vamps out of play at a time, rather
than all of them at once... then you're hopeless. ;) Seriously - Thoughts
Betrayed only makes you unable to use your hand for one vampire, doesn't it?
All your other vampires can still play cards from your hand...

What I want is for remove-vampire-from-game effects to exist as little as
possible, and for them to be reasonably costly and non-straightforward. The
combat method requires at least a few cards, and if you want to make sure they
don't get out of torpor, diablerie (or a master card and a pool, or a skill-
specific action) is required. The mind numb method is a little on the hard-
to-deal-with side for my taste, which may indicate that I have a low tolerance
for non-basic-set effects that are developed (often with, in my opinion,
dubious balance) in later expansions - but Misdirection has a certain amount
of similarity, and is roughly as annoying (and fatal), typically. It's my
opinion that *all* the votes that can remove vampires from the game are a
little excessive - I think the only one my playgroup hasn't messed with is the
Tradition Upheld (successful vote burns a caitiff) one, which inherently is
limited to vampires of cap 1, mostly, with a few 2s and one 3 that I know of
(Dan Murdock - all the Sabbat Pander are not, of course, caitiff).

If Banishment *did* take all your vampires out of play in the same way that
it currently puts one into uncontrolled, it would be broken in ways that TB
can only dream of. TB can get one of your vampires burned, at a fairly high
cost, and you can't play the game while it's happening. Banishing *all* your
vamps with a single vote would most likely get you ousted before you recovered,
at a relatively low opportunity cost (calling and passing a vote), and you
wouldn't get to play the game until you were dead.

A friend of mine pointed out an aspect of banishment that makes it, IMO,
a fairly balanced card. It would be overpowered if not for the two
following aspects.

1. Not only are there two opportunities to stop it from happening, the
initial action which can be blocked, and the vote which can be voted
down. (This has been stated)

2. Bypassing #1 is hopefully easily doable for a vote deck, but can a
good vote deck reliably knock a large vamp down the 3+ blood to make the
vote better than KRC? In my experience a good vote deck will have to
make a big effort (and lose some vamps in the process) to do so much
damage to any large vamp. A good combat deck on the other hand would
have difficulty getting the vote passed (see #1). Ultimately a vote deck
must rely on another player doing the damage to the vamp you wish to
banish. This problem makes banishment a slightly more opportunistic card
that could sometimes find itself without a good target.

Ultimately, banishing any Methusalah's vamp beside your prey's is
pointless unless that vamp is strong enough to threaten you. Anathema on
the other hand applies well to both your predator and your prey and goes
well in a combat deck w/ princes. In the right deck Anathema can be much
more powerful.
